name: Omoplata from Inverted Guard
description: Master the omoplata from inverted guard in BJJ. Complete guide to setup, execution, and finishing this advanced shoulder lock from the inverted position.
target_area: Shoulder joint (rotator cuff, capsule, AC joint)
overview:
The omoplata from inverted guard is an advanced shoulder lock entry that exploits the unique angles created by the inverted position. Unlike standard omoplata entries from closed guard or open guard, the inverted entry uses the practitioner's upside-down orientation to thread the attacking leg over the opponent's shoulder from an unexpected angle. This catches opponents who are focused on defending berimbolo and back take attempts, as the omoplata entry shares initial movements with those transitions.

The technique works best when the opponent reaches forward to control the inverted player's hips or legs, exposing their arm to the leg entanglement. The inverted practitioner threads their far leg over the opponent's shoulder while controlling the wrist, then uses rotational momentum from the inverted position to swing perpendicular and establish the classic omoplata finishing position. The momentum advantage from inversion makes the initial entry faster than traditional setups, though the finishing mechanics remain identical once the perpendicular position is achieved.

Strategically, this technique adds a submission threat to the inverted guard position that forces opponents to respect multiple attack vectors simultaneously. When opponents must defend omoplata entries alongside berimbolo and leg entanglement threats, their defensive decision-making becomes overloaded, creating openings for all three attack categories.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for minor tears, 3-6 months for major tears

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 4-6 seconds minimum pressure increase
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately stop all forward pressure and rotation
Allow opponent to extract arm slowly
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the shoulder rotation
Never apply competition speed in training
Always allow opponent access to tap
Stop immediately if opponent rolls forward (escape attempt)
Never apply full finishing pressure until advanced belt level
Always control the rate of shoulder rotation

attacker.name: from Inverted Guard Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack the omoplata from inverted guard. Step-by-step execution guide with setup details, finishing mechanics, and counter responses.
attacker.overview: Attacking the omoplata from inverted guard requires threading your leg over the opponent's shoulder while inverted, then using rotational momentum to swing into the perpendicular finishing position. The inverted angle creates a faster entry than traditional setups because you generate rotation from the inversion itself rather than having to create it from a static position. The primary challenge is controlling the opponent's posture during the transition from inverted to seated, as any gap in control allows them to stack or posture out. Success depends on maintaining wrist control throughout the rotation and immediately establishing hip control once perpendicular to prevent the forward roll escape.
key_principles: Maintain constant wrist control on the trapped arm throughout the entire entry and finish sequence
Use rotational momentum from inversion rather than muscling into position
Thread the attacking leg deep over the shoulder before initiating the rotation to seated position
Control opponent's hip with your near arm immediately upon reaching perpendicular position
Keep your hips heavy and close to the opponent's shoulder to prevent posture recovery
Angle your body slightly past perpendicular toward the opponent's head to maximize shoulder torque
setup_requirements: Established inverted guard position with shoulder blades on the mat and hips elevated
Opponent reaching forward with at least one arm exposed past your hip line
Wrist or sleeve control on the target arm secured before initiating leg thread
Far leg positioned to swing over opponent's shoulder with sufficient clearance
Opponent's posture broken or weight committed forward to prevent easy disengagement

execution_steps.description: From inverted guard, identify the arm the opponent extends toward your hips or legs. Secure wrist control with your same-side hand while your other hand grips their sleeve or collar to prevent retraction. The arm must be extended past your hip line before proceeding.

Swing your far leg up and over the opponent's shoulder, hooking your hamstring across the back of their neck and shoulder blade. Your calf should drape over their far shoulder while your thigh presses against the near side of their neck. Keep the leg heavy and deep.

Using the momentum from your inverted position, rotate your body away from the opponent to achieve a perpendicular angle. Your hips drive the rotation while your leg clamp on their shoulder maintains arm isolation. Release your supporting hand from the mat as you rotate to seated.

As you arrive perpendicular, immediately reach your near arm across the opponent's lower back and grip their far hip or belt. This hip control is critical because it prevents the primary escape of rolling forward over the trapped shoulder. Without this grip, the finish rate drops dramatically.

Sit up fully with your weight heavy on the trapped arm. Your legs should pinch together with the trapped arm locked between your thigh and calf. Scoot your hips close to the opponent's shoulder so there is no space between your body and theirs. Walk your hips slightly toward their head to increase the angle.

Lean your torso forward over the trapped arm while maintaining hip control. This drives the opponent's shoulder into internal rotation and extension beyond its natural range. Apply pressure slowly and progressively over four to six seconds, allowing time for the tap. The breaking mechanics come from your upper body weight driving the arm toward the mat.

If the initial pressure angle does not produce a tap, walk your hips further toward the opponent's head to increase the rotation angle on the shoulder. You can also pinch your knees tighter together and lift the trapped elbow with your thigh to amplify the shoulder torque. Maintain hip control throughout any adjustment.

common_counters.counter: Opponent postures up and stacks during leg thread
common_counters.your_response: Accelerate the rotation and pull the wrist tight to your chest, using the stacking momentum to assist your swing to perpendicular. If they posture before you thread the leg, abandon and re-establish inverted guard.

common_counters.counter: Opponent rolls forward over trapped shoulder before hip control
common_counters.your_response: Maintain wrist control and follow the roll, transitioning to a mounted omoplata or riding the roll to top position for a sweep. The forward roll only succeeds when hip control is absent, so prioritize that grip.

common_counters.counter: Opponent strips wrist control and retracts arm
common_counters.your_response: Switch to a triangle or armbar entry using the same leg positioning, or recover inverted guard and look for the next opportunity. Chain the omoplata threat with other attacks so arm retraction opens different submissions.

common_counters.counter: Opponent drives forward aggressively to stack and pass
common_counters.your_response: Use the forward drive momentum to accelerate your rotation. If they flatten you before you can rotate, switch to a sweep attempt using the trapped arm as a lever, or recover guard through a granby roll.

common_errors.error: Initiating the leg thread before securing wrist control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent retracts arm during the thread, leaving you in a compromised inverted position with one leg extended and no submission threat
common_errors.correction: Always secure a firm wrist grip before moving the leg. The wrist control is the anchor that makes everything else work. No grip, no attack.

common_errors.error: Failing to control the opponent's hip after reaching perpendicular
common_errors.consequence: Opponent rolls forward over the trapped shoulder, escaping the omoplata and potentially ending in top position or side control
common_errors.correction: The hip control grip must be established within one second of reaching perpendicular. Drill the transition from rotation to hip grip until it becomes automatic.

common_errors.error: Leaving space between your hips and the opponent's shoulder in the finishing position
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can rotate their shoulder or posture to relieve pressure, reducing lock effectiveness and creating escape opportunities
common_errors.correction: Scoot your hips tight against the opponent's shoulder before applying finishing pressure. There should be zero space between your body and their trapped arm.

common_errors.error: Applying finishing pressure too quickly without progressive loading
common_errors.consequence: Risk of sudden shoulder injury to training partner, and the opponent may not have time to tap safely before damage occurs
common_errors.correction: Apply shoulder rotation pressure over 4-6 seconds minimum. Increase force gradually and pause if you feel resistance to allow time for the tap signal.

common_errors.error: Threading the leg too shallow across the shoulder
common_errors.consequence: The leg slides off during rotation, losing the shoulder isolation and wasting the entry attempt entirely
common_errors.correction: Drive your hamstring deep across the back of the opponent's neck so your calf passes their far shoulder completely. A deeper thread creates a stronger clamp.

common_errors.error: Losing inverted base during the initial setup by reaching too far
common_errors.consequence: Weight shifts to neck instead of shoulders, creating cervical injury risk and making the entry sluggish with poor rotation mechanics
common_errors.correction: Maintain proper shoulder blade contact with the mat throughout setup. If you feel neck pressure, reset your base before attempting the leg thread.

training_progressions.description: Practice inverting from guard position and rotating to seated without a partner. Focus on smooth shoulder-to-hip transitions, maintaining weight on shoulder blades, and building the specific hip rotation pattern needed for the omoplata swing. 10-15 reps per side.

training_progressions.focus: Full technique sequence with passive partner
training_progressions.description: Drill the complete entry from inverted guard through the finish with a non-resisting partner. Emphasis on wrist control timing, leg thread depth, rotation mechanics, and hip control establishment. Partner provides body positioning feedback. 20-30 reps per session.

training_progressions.focus: Timing and control against increasing defense
training_progressions.description: Partner provides graduated resistance at specific decision points: posturing during setup, attempting forward roll during finish, stripping wrist control. Develop real-time adjustments and counter-to-counter sequences. 10-minute positional rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Combining with berimbolo and triangle threats
training_progressions.description: Drill the omoplata as part of the full inverted guard attack chain. Start with berimbolo entry, if defended switch to omoplata, if that is defended switch to triangle. Develop the ability to read defensive reactions and flow between attacks. Live sparring rounds starting from inverted guard.

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structure does the omoplata from inverted guard primarily attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The omoplata attacks the shoulder joint complex, specifically targeting the rotator cuff muscles and tendons through forced internal rotation and extension beyond the joint's natural range. The primary stress falls on the supraspinatus, infraspinatus, and subscapularis tendons, with secondary pressure on the AC joint and shoulder capsule. The lever created by your legs against the opponent's upper arm forces the humeral head into a compromised position within the glenoid fossa.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts to posture up as you thread your leg over their shoulder - what adjustment prevents escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Pull their wrist sharply to your chest while simultaneously accelerating your leg thread and hip rotation. The posturing motion actually assists your rotation if you use their upward momentum to swing to perpendicular faster. Clamp your legs tight the moment you feel them rising and use their posture break attempt as energy for your own transition. If they posture before your leg is threaded, abort and re-establish inverted guard rather than forcing a compromised entry.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the point of no escape for the opponent during the omoplata from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The point of no escape occurs when you have achieved perpendicular positioning with hip control established and your hips scooted tight against the opponent's shoulder. Once the hip control grip prevents their forward roll and your body weight is loaded onto the trapped arm with no space between your hips and their shoulder, the only remaining option is to tap. Before this point, they can still roll forward, posture, or strip grips to escape.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the key safety considerations when applying the omoplata from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Apply finishing pressure slowly over 4-6 seconds minimum with progressive loading. Never jerk or spike the shoulder rotation. Always maintain awareness of tap signals including verbal taps, physical taps on your body or the mat, and any distress sounds. If the opponent attempts to roll forward, release immediately as continuing pressure during a roll creates severe shoulder injury risk. In training, never apply competition-level speed or intensity on the finish.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should you release the omoplata from inverted guard after a tap?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately stop all forward pressure on the trapped arm and cease hip rotation. Release the leg clamp by separating your knees and lifting your top leg off the opponent's shoulder. Unwind your hip position back to neutral. Allow the opponent to extract their arm at their own pace without rushing or pulling it free, as the shoulder may be compromised. Check with your partner about any pain or injury before resuming training.

knowledge_assessment.question: What grip adjustment should you make if the standard finish angle is not producing a tap?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Walk your hips further toward the opponent's head to increase the rotational angle on the shoulder joint. Additionally, pinch your knees tighter together and use your top thigh to lift the opponent's trapped elbow upward, amplifying the lever effect. You can also shift your lean angle from directly forward to slightly diagonal toward the opponent's head, which changes the torque vector on the shoulder. Ensure hip control remains solid throughout any adjustment.

knowledge_assessment.question: What makes the inverted guard entry for the omoplata different from a standard closed guard omoplata entry?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The inverted entry uses the existing rotational momentum from the inverted position to swing into the perpendicular finishing angle, making the initial entry faster than the standard setup which requires generating rotation from a static closed guard. The leg thread comes from above the opponent's shoulder rather than from the side, creating an unexpected angle that bypasses standard omoplata defenses. However, the inverted entry carries higher risk because you must transition from an unstable inverted base to a stable seated finish.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you chain the omoplata with other attacks from inverted guard when the opponent defends?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If the opponent defends the omoplata by retracting their arm, the same leg positioning sets up a triangle by switching to control the opposite side of their neck. If they posture aggressively, redirect to a berimbolo entry using the momentum they create. If they drive forward, sweep them using the trapped arm as a lever. The omoplata, triangle, berimbolo, and sweep share initial movements from inverted guard, so each defense opens the next attack in the chain.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the most common finishing error that reduces omoplata effectiveness from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The most common finishing error is leaving space between your hips and the opponent's trapped shoulder. This gap allows the opponent to rotate their shoulder internally, reducing the torque applied by your body weight. It also gives them room to start posturing or shifting their weight to set up a roll escape. The correction is to scoot your hips flush against their shoulder before applying any forward pressure, eliminating all space in the finishing position.

knowledge_assessment.question: During competition, how should you time the omoplata entry from inverted guard for maximum effectiveness?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Time the entry when the opponent commits their weight forward to address your inverted guard, specifically when they reach to control your hips or attempt a passing grip. Their forward commitment creates the arm exposure needed for the leg thread and their momentum assists your rotation. Avoid attempting the entry when the opponent maintains distance or has their weight back, as they can simply disengage. The best window is during their transition from standing to engaged passing posture.

defender.name: from Inverted Guard Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend and escape the omoplata from inverted guard. Recognition cues, escape timing, and defensive strategies to prevent the shoulder lock.
defender.overview: Defending the omoplata from inverted guard requires recognizing the setup early and responding before the attacker completes the rotation to perpendicular. The inverted entry is faster than standard omoplata setups because the attacker uses existing rotational momentum, so defensive reactions must be immediate. The primary defensive windows occur during the leg thread before it crosses your shoulder, during the rotation before they reach perpendicular, and during the finish via the forward roll escape. Understanding which window you are in determines which defense is appropriate. Late-stage defense is significantly harder and riskier than early recognition and prevention.
key_principles: Keep elbows tight to your body and avoid reaching forward with extended arms when engaging inverted guard
Recognize the leg thread over your shoulder as the earliest warning sign and immediately retract the threatened arm
Maintain upright posture and resist being pulled forward into the inverted player's rotation
If caught in the omoplata rotation, immediately begin posturing before the attacker establishes hip control
The forward roll escape must be executed before hip control is established or it will be blocked
Control the attacker's far hip during escape attempts to prevent them from following your movement
recognition_cues: Opponent secures wrist or sleeve control on your arm while inverted and begins elevating their far leg toward your shoulder
You feel your arm being pulled toward the opponent's hip while their leg swings over your shoulder and hamstring crosses behind your neck
Opponent's body begins rotating from inverted to perpendicular with your arm trapped between their legs
Increasing pressure on the back of your neck from the opponent's hamstring crossing over your shoulder blade

defensive_options.action: Retract arm and posture up immediately upon feeling wrist control from inverted opponent
defensive_options.when_to_use: Early stage - before the opponent threads their leg over your shoulder
defensive_options.if_successful: Opponent remains in inverted guard with no submission threat and must reset their attack
defensive_options.risk: Low risk if timed correctly. If too late, you may be pulled into the rotation with arm extended.

defensive_options.action: Stack and drive forward through the rotation to flatten the inverted player and pass
defensive_options.when_to_use: Mid stage - during the leg thread or early rotation before perpendicular is achieved
defensive_options.if_successful: You flatten the opponent and pass to side control, completely negating the submission threat
defensive_options.risk: Medium risk. Driving forward can accelerate the attacker's rotation if they maintain wrist control and redirect your momentum.

defensive_options.action: Forward roll over trapped shoulder before hip control is established by the attacker
defensive_options.when_to_use: Late stage - attacker has reached perpendicular but has not yet secured hip control grip
defensive_options.if_successful: You escape the omoplata and end up in a scramble or return to a neutral position
defensive_options.risk: High risk. If the attacker already has hip control, the roll is blocked and you waste energy in a worse position.

escape_paths: Early arm retraction with posture recovery to reset the guard engagement
Forward roll over trapped shoulder before hip control is secured
Stack pass through the rotation to flatten opponent and achieve side control
Limp arm the trapped shoulder to reduce torque and create space for extraction

favorable_outcomes.how: Stack the inverted player aggressively during their rotation, driving your weight through their legs to flatten them and pass directly to side control top position

common_errors.error: Reaching forward with extended arms when engaging the inverted guard player
common_errors.consequence: Arms become exposed targets for omoplata, triangle, and armbar entries from the inverted position
common_errors.correction: Keep elbows pinched to your ribs when engaging inverted guard. Only extend arms with purpose and retract immediately after grip establishment.

common_errors.error: Attempting the forward roll escape after the attacker has established hip control
common_errors.consequence: Roll is blocked by the hip grip, wasting energy and leaving you in a worse position with the submission fully locked
common_errors.correction: Only attempt the forward roll in the window before hip control is established. If hip control is already secured, focus on posturing and creating space instead.

common_errors.error: Panicking and pulling the trapped arm outward instead of turning into the attacker
common_errors.consequence: Outward pulling increases the rotational torque on the shoulder and accelerates the submission
common_errors.correction: Turn your body toward the attacker and drive your shoulder forward to reduce the angle. Pulling away makes the omoplata tighter, not looser.

common_errors.error: Dropping to knees when feeling the leg thread instead of maintaining base and posture
common_errors.consequence: Kneeling removes your ability to posture and creates a stable platform for the attacker to complete the rotation
common_errors.correction: Stay on your feet or in combat base. Your legs are your primary tool for posturing out of the omoplata entry. Maintain upright posture and driving capability.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you recognize that an omoplata from inverted guard is being set up?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary recognition cues are the opponent securing wrist or sleeve control on your arm while inverted, followed by their far leg beginning to elevate and swing toward your shoulder. You will feel a pulling force on your wrist directing your arm across their body, and increasing pressure on the back of your neck as their hamstring crosses over your shoulder. Early recognition at the wrist control stage gives you the best defensive window.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the safest way to tap to the omoplata from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap clearly and repeatedly using your free hand on the opponent's body, the mat, or your own body. Verbal taps are equally valid and should be used if your free hand is trapped. Tap early when you feel the shoulder reaching its rotational limit rather than waiting for pain, as the shoulder joint can sustain damage before significant pain registers. If you cannot tap with your hands, tap with your feet or verbalize loudly.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive options are available against the omoplata from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Three primary defensive options exist depending on timing. Early stage: retract the threatened arm and posture up before the leg threads over your shoulder. Mid stage: stack and drive forward to flatten the inverted player during their rotation. Late stage: forward roll over the trapped shoulder before the attacker secures hip control. Each defense is only effective within its specific timing window, and attempting the wrong defense for the current stage dramatically reduces success.

knowledge_assessment.question: Why is the forward roll escape ineffective once hip control is established?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The hip control grip on your far hip or belt acts as an anchor that prevents your body from completing the forward rotation. When the attacker controls your hip, your rolling momentum is absorbed by their grip and your body cannot complete the rotation needed to escape. Attempting to force the roll against hip control drives your trapped shoulder deeper into the submission angle, making the position worse instead of better.

knowledge_assessment.question: What body positioning prevents the initial omoplata setup from inverted guard?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Keep elbows tight to your body and avoid reaching forward when engaging the inverted guard player. Maintain an upright posture with your base wide and weight distributed back rather than leaning forward. When gripping, use short controlled reaches and retract immediately after. If you must engage their legs to pass, use your elbows rather than extended hands, and keep your chin tucked to prevent your head from being used as a control point.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying omoplata setups from inverted guard
training_progressions.description: Partner slowly executes the omoplata entry sequence from inverted guard while you practice recognizing each stage: wrist control, leg thread, rotation, hip control. Call out each stage as you recognize it. Build pattern recognition before adding defensive responses.

training_progressions.focus: Arm retraction and posture recovery timing
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts omoplata entries at increasing speeds while you practice the early defense of arm retraction and posture recovery. Focus on the timing window between wrist control and leg thread. Develop the reflex to retract immediately upon feeling wrist control from an inverted opponent.

training_progressions.focus: Forward roll and stack escapes against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Drill the forward roll escape and stack pass defense from progressively later stages of the omoplata entry. Partner increases resistance and adds hip control. Learn to assess which escape is available based on the stage and commit fully to the chosen defense.

training_progressions.focus: Full defense against live omoplata attacks from inverted guard
training_progressions.description: Positional sparring rounds starting with opponent in inverted guard. Defend all attacks including omoplata, berimbolo, and triangles. Develop real-time decision making about which threats to prioritize and which defensive responses match the current attack.
